lessons.title: The three stages of labor
lessons.why: Knowing the shape of it makes it far less frightening in the moment.
facts: Stage 1: contractions dilate the cervix from 0 to 10cm — the longest stage, often 8–14 hours for a first baby.
Stage 2: pushing and delivery of the baby — usually 20 minutes to a few hours.
Stage 3: delivery of the placenta — typically 5–30 minutes after birth.

lessons.title: Signs of true labor vs. Braxton Hicks
lessons.why: False alarms are common in the last weeks — this is how to tell the difference.
facts: True contractions get closer together, longer, and stronger over time; Braxton Hicks stay irregular and often ease with rest or hydration.
True labor pain doesn't go away with a position change; Braxton Hicks often do.
Other real signs: your water breaking, or a "bloody show" (mucus plug with light spotting).
lessons.mustRemember: Call your care team if contractions are 5 minutes apart, lasting 1 minute, for 1 hour ("5-1-1") — or immediately if your water breaks.

lessons.title: When to head to the hospital
lessons.why: Leaving too early or too late are both common regrets.
facts: Follow the 5-1-1 rule for first labors, but go sooner if your hospital is far or it's not your first baby.
Go immediately for: water breaking, heavy bleeding, reduced fetal movement, or severe unrelenting pain.
Call the hospital/clinic first — they may want you to come straight in rather than wait out contractions at home.

lessons.title: Pain relief options
lessons.why: Deciding roughly what you want beforehand reduces stress mid-labor.
facts: Epidural: regional anesthesia, most common, doesn't fully remove sensation but numbs most pain.
Nitrous oxide (gas & air): short-acting, self-administered, wears off fast.
Non-medical: breathing techniques, water immersion, movement, massage from a birth partner.

lessons.title: The birth partner's real job
lessons.why: This is what actually helps versus what looks helpful in movies.
facts: Advocate: relay her wishes to staff when she can't easily speak for herself.
Track time: note contraction frequency and duration so you have real numbers when calling the hospital.
Stay calm and present — your steadiness is often more valuable than anything you say.

lessons.title: C-section basics
lessons.why: Roughly 1 in 3 births in Singapore involve a C-section — worth understanding even if unplanned.
facts: Can be planned (breech position, placenta previa, prior C-section) or unplanned (labor stalls, fetal distress).
Recovery is longer than vaginal birth — typically 4–6 weeks, with limits on lifting and driving.
A support partner is usually allowed in the room for both planned and emergency C-sections in Singapore.

lessons.title: Newborn feeding cues
lessons.why: Newborns signal hunger well before crying — catching it early makes feeds calmer.
facts: Early cues: rooting (turning head, mouth open), sucking on hands, smacking lips.
Crying is a late cue — by then the baby is already distressed and harder to latch.
Expect 8–12 feeds per 24 hours in the first weeks, whether breast or bottle.

lessons.title: Umbilical cord stump care
lessons.why: Simple, but a common source of new-parent anxiety.
facts: Keep it dry and exposed to air — fold diapers below it, and stick to sponge baths until it falls off.
It typically falls off on its own within 1–3 weeks. Some blood-tinged discharge right before is normal.
Call your pediatrician if you see pus, redness spreading to the skin, or a foul smell.

lessons.title: Bathing a newborn
lessons.why: You don't need to (and shouldn't) bathe a newborn every day.
facts: 2–3 times a week is enough before the baby is mobile — daily bathing can dry out their skin.
Sponge baths only until the umbilical cord falls off.
Keep water lukewarm (around 37°C) and never leave the baby unattended, even for a second.
lessons.mustRemember: Never leave a baby alone in bath water — not even to grab a towel. Bring everything within arm's reach first.

lessons.title: Diapering essentials
lessons.why: You'll do this 8–10 times a day — worth doing efficiently.
facts: Change before or right after feeds, and immediately after a bowel movement.
For boys, point the penis downward before closing the diaper to avoid leaks upward.
Watch for diaper rash — treat early with a barrier cream and more frequent changes.

modules.label: Crying & Soothing
modules.summary: Crying is communication, not danger — work the checklist first, then reach for the 5 S's.

lessons.title: The quick checklist before anything else
lessons.why: Most crying has a simple, fixable cause — check these before assuming something's wrong.
facts: Hungry — the most common cause, especially in the first weeks.
Tired, wet or soiled, too hot or too cold, or simply wants to be held.
Overstimulated — sometimes a quiet, dim room is the fix, not more input.

lessons.title: The 5 S's: the idea
lessons.why: Dr. Harvey Karp's "5 S's" recreate the womb environment and reliably trigger a newborn's calming reflex.
facts: Swaddle, side/stomach hold, shush, swing, and suck — five specific techniques, not a random list.
Each one mimics a condition in the womb: snugness, being held, constant whooshing noise, motion, sucking.
Try them together rather than one at a time — most parents find a combination works better than any single S alone.

media.caption: The 5 S's to Soothe Your Baby — Dr. Harvey Karp, Happiest Baby

lessons.title: S #1: Swaddle
lessons.why: Recreates the snugness of the womb and stops a baby's own startle reflex from waking them back up.
facts: Wrap snugly with arms in; leave room at the hips for legs to bend up and out, frog-style.
Snug at the chest, looser at the hips — swaddling the legs too tightly raises hip dysplasia risk.
Stop swaddling for sleep the moment baby shows signs of rolling — a swaddled roll is a suffocation risk.

media.caption: Swaddle Your Baby Like a Pro: Pediatrician Tips

lessons.title: S #2: Side or stomach hold
lessons.why: A different position and belly pressure than an upright cradle hold — often calms a baby a cradle hold doesn't.
facts: Hold baby on their side or stomach along your forearm, supporting the head and neck.
This is for soothing while awake and supervised only — never a sleep position.
Sleep must always be on the back, alone, in the crib (see Safe Sleep Basics) — this hold is just for calming.

lessons.title: S #3: Shush
lessons.why: Newborns just spent 9 months next to the loud whoosh of blood flow — near-silence is unfamiliar, not soothing.
facts: A loud, continuous "shhh" held right next to baby's ear — louder than most parents expect at first.
A white-noise machine or app works too, as long as it's loud and continuous rather than soft and intermittent.
Match the shush volume to how hard the baby is crying, then taper it down gradually as they calm.

lessons.title: S #4: Swing
lessons.why: Stillness is the least womb-like state — motion is what most reliably keeps the calming reflex switched on.
facts: Small, fast, rhythmic motion — a tight jiggle, not a big slow rock.
Always support the head and neck fully; the motion should never be a shake or a jerk.
Once baby is calm, the motion can be slowed down gradually rather than stopped abruptly.

lessons.title: S #5: Suck
lessons.why: Sucking triggers one of the strongest newborn calming reflexes, separate from actual hunger.
facts: A pacifier or a clean finger works if baby isn't due for a feed.
Offering the breast or bottle works too, if you're not trying to avoid comfort-feeding.
Often the most effective added last, once the other S's have already gotten baby partway calm.

lessons.title: Purple crying is real, and it's not your fault
lessons.why: Some crying has no fixable cause at all — knowing this in advance heads off a lot of self-blame.
facts: "Purple crying" is a normal stretch of unexplained, hard-to-soothe crying that peaks around 6 weeks.
It usually resolves on its own by 3–4 months, regardless of what soothing method you use.
It's named and taught specifically to prevent shaken baby syndrome — the crying is not a sign you're doing something wrong.
lessons.mustRemember: If nothing is working and you feel your own frustration rising, it's safe to put baby down in the crib and step away for a few minutes. Never shake a baby.

media.caption: The Period of PURPLE Crying — National Center on Shaken Baby Syndrome

modules.takeaway: If nothing is working after a real effort, it's safe to put baby down in the crib and step away for a few minutes. Never shake a baby.

modules.label: Sleep
modules.summary: Newborn sleep looks chaotic by adult standards — that's normal, not a sign anything's wrong.

lessons.title: How much newborns actually sleep
lessons.why: Knowing the real numbers ahead of time stops you from panicking over something that's completely normal.
facts: Newborns sleep 14–17 hours a day in total.
But rarely more than 2–4 hours at a single stretch, day or night.
This comes from their small stomachs and short sleep cycles — not something you can train away early on.

lessons.title: Fixing day/night confusion
lessons.why: Newborns are born with no sense of day and night — you have to help them learn it.
facts: Being more alert at night and sleepier by day is normal in the first weeks.
Bright light and activity during the day, dim and quiet at night, help reset the body clock.
It typically resolves within a few weeks as their circadian rhythm matures.

lessons.title: Starting a wind-down routine early
lessons.why: The specific routine matters less than starting the habit of one, consistently, from day one.
facts: A short, consistent wind-down (dim lights, swaddle, quiet) can start from week one.
Consistency matters more than the exact steps — babies respond to the pattern repeating.
It won't produce a predictable schedule yet, but it lays the groundwork for one later.

modules.takeaway: Expect fragmented, unpredictable sleep for months — focus on safety (see Safe Sleep Basics), not a schedule, for now.

lessons.title: What "recovery" actually looks like
lessons.why: Films skip this — the reality is a longer process than most people expect.
facts: Vaginal bleeding (lochia) can last 4–6 weeks, tapering from bright red to brown to yellow-white.
Full physical recovery, especially after a C-section, is closer to 6–8 weeks minimum.
Afterpains (uterus contracting back down) are normal and often stronger with each subsequent baby.

lessons.title: Baby blues vs. postpartum depression
lessons.why: One is expected and passes; the other needs professional support — telling them apart matters.
facts: "Baby blues" affects up to 80% of new mothers: mood swings, weepiness, anxiety in the first 2 weeks.
Postpartum depression (PPD) lasts longer than 2 weeks and is more intense — persistent sadness, hopelessness, difficulty bonding.
PPD is treatable and common — it affects fathers/partners too, and screening is available through your polyclinic or hospital.
lessons.mustRemember: If low mood lasts beyond 2 weeks, or includes thoughts of harming yourself or the baby, contact a doctor immediately — this is medical, not a personal failing.

lessons.title: Pelvic floor recovery
lessons.why: Often skipped in prep, but affects long-term comfort and health.
facts: Pelvic floor muscles are stretched by pregnancy and vaginal delivery, and weakened even after C-sections.
Gentle pelvic floor exercises can typically start within days postpartum, but check with your obstetrician first.
Singapore hospitals and polyclinics offer postnatal physiotherapy referrals — worth asking about at your 6-week check.

lessons.title: Sex and intimacy after birth
lessons.why: Timelines vary widely — this removes the guesswork.
facts: Most doctors advise waiting until after the 6-week postpartum check before resuming penetrative sex.
Hormonal changes (especially while breastfeeding) can reduce libido and cause vaginal dryness — this is temporary and normal.
Non-sexual intimacy and communication matter more in this window than most couples expect.

lessons.title: Building your support system now
lessons.why: The best time to arrange help is before you need it desperately.
facts: Decide in advance who's doing what in the first 2 weeks: meals, errands, night wake-ups, visitors.
If hiring a confinement nanny or postpartum doula, book 2–3 months ahead — good ones are fully booked early in Singapore.
Agree with your partner on a "tag out" signal for when either of you is overwhelmed, before you're in the moment.

lessons.title: Hospital bag checklist
lessons.why: Pack by week 36 — babies don't wait for your to-do list.
facts: For mum: ID/passport, insurance card, maternity pads, nursing bra, comfortable going-home outfit, phone charger.
For baby: going-home outfit, swaddle/blanket, car seat installed in the car beforehand.
For partner: snacks, change of clothes, entertainment for long stretches of waiting, cash/cards for parking and food.

lessons.title: Paternity & shared parental leave (2026 rules)
lessons.why: This changed recently — worth knowing the current numbers, not the ones from a few years ago.
facts: Fathers of Singapore-citizen children get 4 weeks of Government-Paid Paternity Leave (GPPL), mandatory since April 2025.
From 1 April 2026, an additional Shared Parental Leave (SPL) pool of 10 weeks is split between both parents (5 weeks each by default, reallocatable).
Combined with 16 weeks of maternity leave, eligible families can access up to 30 weeks of paid leave in baby's first year — leave must generally be used within 12 months of birth.

lessons.title: Registering the birth
lessons.why: There's a hard deadline most new parents don't know about.
facts: Births in Singapore must be registered within 42 days at the Registry of Births and Deaths (usually done at the hospital before discharge).
You'll need both parents' NRICs/passports and the marriage certificate (if applicable).
The birth certificate is required to open a CDA account and apply for Baby Bonus.
lessons.mustRemember: Register the birth within 42 days — most hospitals help you do this before discharge, so ask about it on admission.

lessons.title: Baby Bonus & CDA account
lessons.why: Free government money that requires you to actively apply for it.
facts: The Baby Bonus cash gift and Child Development Account (CDA) require an online application after the birth is registered.
The CDA is a co-savings account — government matches your contributions up to a cap, usable for approved childcare/medical expenses.
Apply promptly — some components have time-sensitive application windows.

lessons.title: Choosing a pediatrician
lessons.why: Better to decide before you're sleep-deprived and need one urgently.
facts: Ask your gynae or hospital for a referral, or check which pediatric clinics are near home for late-night visits.
Confirm which hospital they're affiliated with, in case of admission.
Newborns typically need checkups at 1 week, 1 month, and then at regular intervals — book the first one before discharge.

lessons.title: Insurance to sort before birth
lessons.why: Some policies need to be in place before the baby arrives to avoid pre-existing condition exclusions.
facts: MediShield Life covers newborns automatically from birth for Singapore citizens/PRs, but check if you want additional Integrated Shield Plan coverage.
Congenital conditions are sometimes excluded unless you apply for coverage within a set window after birth — check the exact deadline with your insurer.
Confirm what your hospital plan covers for delivery (ward class, complications, NICU stay) before you're admitted.

lessons.title: Safe sleep basics
lessons.why: This single set of guidelines has the biggest evidence base for reducing SIDS risk.
facts: Back to sleep, every sleep, for the first year.
Firm, flat mattress in the crib/bassinet — no pillows, blankets, bumpers, or soft toys.
Room-sharing (not bed-sharing) for at least the first 6 months is recommended.
lessons.mustRemember: Back, flat, bare crib — every single sleep, including naps.

lessons.title: Car seat basics
lessons.why: Most parents install it wrong the first time — worth checking properly.
facts: Rear-facing car seat is mandatory in Singapore for infants, in the back seat.
The seat should be installed with no more than 2.5cm of movement side to side when tugged at the base.
Many workshops and some hospitals in Singapore offer free car seat installation checks — worth booking one before week 36.

lessons.title: Infant CPR & choking response
lessons.why: A skill you hope to never use, but one course removes most of the panic if you ever do.
facts: Infant CPR and choking response differ meaningfully from adult/child techniques — hands-on training beats reading about it.
Singapore Red Cross and SGH/KKH often run short infant first aid courses for expecting parents.
Aim to complete a certified course before the due date, ideally with both parents attending together.

lessons.title: Babyproofing timeline
lessons.why: You don't need to do it all on day one — but some things matter early.
facts: Before birth: safe sleep setup, smoke detectors working, water heater temperature capped to avoid scalds.
By 4–6 months (rolling starts): outlet covers, secure furniture that could tip, remove small choking hazards from floor level.
By 8–9 months (crawling/pulling up): stair gates, cabinet locks, cord/blind safety, corner guards on sharp furniture.
